newsitem.title: FRANCE: Unemployment overshadows France's EMU dream.
newsitem.headline: Unemployment overshadows France's EMU dream.

text.p: France ought to be celebrating. Growth is picking up, foreign trade is booming and its political ambition of a single European currency seems within reach.
But the good news is overshadowed by unemployment, with more than one in eight people out of work.

Figures due on Friday are likely to show the total jobless numbers climbed higher in February, economists say, while this week national statistics institute INSEE forecast the jobless rate would climb to 12.9 percent in June from 12.7 percent now.

At the same time, company restructuring to compete in an increasingly globalised market, such as carmaker Renault's decision to close a Belgian plant and cut 2,764 jobs in France, is producing scary media headlines.

"Looking at France from the outside you would think the country is going down the drain. But when you look at the numbers you see significant signs of improvement," BIP economist Marie-Owens Thomsen said.

The rise in unemployment is slowing, and with growth accelerating, the trend should reverse towards the end of the year, giving the government something to celebrate as it goes into parliamentary elections in March 1998.
Economists believe economic growth will pick up speed later this year and into next year. The government expects growth of at least 2.3 percent this year after 1.3 percent last year.

After that, a successful launch of a single currency in 1999 would put Europe on a path for healthy sustainable growth for some years to come, after years of recession and anaemic growth as it wrestled with spending cuts and currency turbulence.

For many French economists, growth is the main key to bringing down unemployment, while talk of a need to remodel the country along "Anglo-Saxon" lines, with a more flexible labour market, is a secondary issue.
"Fundamentally you need growth to change anything," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.

They argue that the United States took some time to create jobs when it came out of recession in 1991, but it has since enjoyed a stronger and longer period of growth than Europe by following an expansionist policy which also boosted jobs.

"If we were able to have growth above 2 1/2 percent for 10 years that could reduce unemployment to five percent," Thomsen said. But, she added, that was not going to happen and growth would in any case have to be accompanied by reforms.
And the 3.1 million people out of work will have to wait a while to see the situation improve enough to help them.
Economists say unemployment, traditionally hard to forecast, is likely to have crept up in February by some 5,000 to 12,000, after rising in January by 18,100 to 3.1 million.
The February rise would probably not be enough to push up the jobless rate beyond 12.7 percent.

But this is nonetheless expected to rise further in later months, peaking at around 13 percent before turning around towards the end of the year and perhaps even sinking below the symbolic 12 percent level before the 1998 elections.
Job creation does appear to be improving, slowing the rise in unemployment -- which even dropped in October and December.
But France's demographics have meant its active population is increasing faster than it can create jobs.

"That is what is making things difficult, because even when the economy works better, starts creating jobs again, we have some trouble being sufficiently creative to absorb this new population," Prime Minister Alain Juppe said this month.
Finding that creativity has flummoxed most politicians.
President Jacques Chirac took office in 1995 promising to make jobs a priority. But his government quickly became bogged down in a myriad of failed subsidised job-creation schemes.
Now Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, launching the opposition's programme for 1998, is saying France needs shock treatment to boost growth and cut unemployment.

But his promise to create 700,000 jobs looked remarkably similar to pledges of previous governments, and his aim of cutting the working week without cutting pay looks too out of tune with current thinking to have much chance of early success.
That leaves prospects for growth as the best hope for the unemployed.
